tldr: A strong clinician gets passed over for three specific reasons, and none of them is that you can't do the job. Six questions do most of the screening, and each has a shape of answer that works and a common answer that disqualifies you.

blocks.text: The question underneath a first non-clinical interview is whether you will still be there in a year, or whether you will miss the kids and go back. Hiring managers rarely say it out loud. They ask something softer and listen for the answer anyway.
You are being sorted against three doubts
A strong clinician gets passed over for the same three reasons, and each one has an answer you can build this week.

items.title: Will you go back?
items.text: Six years of training and a licence look like a strong pull backward. Show that leaving was a decision with your pull sentence from lesson 1.8.

items.title: Words they cannot map
items.text: Caseload and IEP mean nothing outside healthcare. Say portfolio, stakeholders, outcomes and adoption, the words on their job posting (lesson 4.2).

items.title: No proof you invested
items.text: Anyone can say they are interested. Bring one thing you made on your own time: a Rise module, a rebuilt spreadsheet, a one-page workflow write-up (lesson 5.2).

blocks.text: A fourth, quieter doubt is that your salary expectations sit somewhere they cannot reach. Lesson 6.5 handles that one.
lots of prospective employees are skeptical about my actually wanting to transition into a different career field because of my background
Build every answer from three parts, and leave out what went wrong
Every answer to a career-change question has the same three parts, in the same order.

blocks.title: The shape of a good answer

items.label: How you prepared
items.note: what you built and who you talked to

items.label: One result
items.note: a number that maps onto a problem in their first ninety days

blocks.text: Nothing in that shape explains what went wrong. Burnout, caseload size, productivity percentages and documentation hours are all true, and each one confirms the doubt you came to answer.

blocks.title: A line that works in customer success
blocks.text: One transitioner opens with a version of this: I have been doing customer success my whole career, I just called it patient and family care. Then a metric. One sentence reframes the whole résumé, and the number proves it.
Answer "tell me about yourself" in forty-five seconds
Most interviews open with this question, and most people wing it. Give your pitch, then your pull, then one number.

blocks.title: The opener
blocks.text: I've been an SLP for [N] years, mostly in [setting]. The part I've been best at, and the part I want to do all day, is [the two things]. In [month] I started [the preparation: the course, the module, the conversations], and I applied here because [the specific thing about the role]. The number I'm proudest of is [one accomplishment with a figure].
Point every sentence at the work you would do here
Eager and desperate are both true feelings, and only eager gets hired. A desperate sentence points at what you are leaving, and an eager one points at the work in front of you.

blocks.title: The same wish, two ways
blocks.before: Honestly I'd take anything that isn't a caseload. I'm so done.
blocks.after: I learned [the thing] in clinical work, and this is the role where I get to use it all day. It's the right fit because [A], [B] and [C].

blocks.text: Close the interview by asking for the next step: "What happens next, and is there anything else I can send you in the meantime?"
Prepare for six questions, because they do most of the screening
The questions a career changer gets are predictable. These six turn up in phone screens, on application forms and in the first ten minutes with a hiring manager.

items.title: Why are you leaving?
items.text: Works: one sentence of pull, one of the preparation you have done. Sinks: any sentence that starts with what you are escaping. They hear a retention risk.

items.title: Why should we consider you?
items.text: Works: two accomplishments with numbers, mapped onto the role's first ninety days. Sinks: a list of soft skills. "Communication" answers nothing.

items.title: Do you know our product?
items.text: Works: one specific thing you found by using it or talking to a customer, and one question it raised. Sinks: reciting the About page.

items.title: Where in three years?
items.text: Works: inside this function, with a bigger scope, the next title named honestly. Sinks: a joke about going back to clinical, or a title from another department.

items.title: Your salary expectation?
items.text: Works: ask their budgeted range, or give the documented range for your path (lesson 6.5). Sinks: naming your clinical salary first.

items.title: A difficult stakeholder?
items.text: Works: a parent or administrator story with the objection, what you changed and the outcome. Sinks: a story that ends with you being right.

blocks.text: An answer to the second question sounds like this: "I've been doing customer success my whole career. I called it family care. [N] families at a time, a plan and a quarterly review for each, and [your real result]."
Describe an event with a number in it, never a quality

A strong answer uses the vocabulary of the role and holds one number that could be checked. A weak one reaches for a quality: communication skills, detail-oriented, works well under pressure, passionate about helping people. Nearly every applicant claims those, and they prove nothing about any of them.

blocks.title: A behavioural answer, twice
blocks.before: I'm great with difficult parents. I always stay calm and find common ground.
blocks.after: A parent refused an AAC trial for four months because she thought it would stop her son talking. I brought her the research, then a two-week trial with a defined stop point. She agreed to the trial and requested the device herself at week three.

blocks.text: The second answer has an objection, an intervention and an outcome, and a customer success manager hears their own job description in it.
Keep five lines ready for the moments that derail people
The moments that derail an interview are small and predictable, so have the sentence ready.

items.title: A term you don't know
items.text: "I'm not familiar with that one. Is it similar to [the closest thing you do know]?"

items.title: Your nerves are showing
items.text: "Sorry, I'm excited about this role and my nerves are getting ahead of me. Let me start that again."

items.title: A tool you haven't used
items.text: "I haven't used [tool] in a job. I've [built one thing in it], and I've learned every [EMR / scheduling platform] I was handed on the job."

items.title: A question from left field
items.text: Answer it like a person. They are checking whether you are one.

items.title: Your last question
items.text: Only if you can hear the answer: "Is there anything about my background that gives you pause? I'd like the chance to address it."

blocks.text: Use the text box on an application form to bridge, never to apologise

The knockout questions on an application form are the real automatic filter: years of experience in the field, a named certification, authorisation to work without sponsorship. Answer them honestly. Where a form gives you a text box, use it to connect your clinical work to the role.

blocks.title: Write the screening answers yourself
blocks.text: One hiring manager reported that 35 percent of applicants submitted identical AI-generated answers to the screening questions. A screening box is the cheapest place in the whole process to sound like a person.
Write out the two answers you would fumble today
Write both answers longhand, then cut them by half. Short and specific beats complete.

items.q: On a phone screen, a recruiter asks why you are leaving the schools. Which opening helps you most?
options: My caseload hit 62 across three buildings, and nobody can sustain that.
I want to work on how services get delivered, and I built a Rise module to test whether I like the work.
I've always been a strong communicator and a fast learner.
items.why: It starts with where you are going and adds preparation. The first confirms the retention doubt, and the third names a quality instead of an event.

items.q: The interviewer names a tool you have never used. What do you say?
options: That you are familiar with it, and then you learn it before your start date.
That you haven't used it in a job, what you have built or studied, and the systems you picked up on the job.
That clinical work never needed it, with an apology.
items.why: An honest gap plus evidence that you learn systems answers the doubt, and a bluff fails at the first follow-up question.

blocks.label: The two questions you'd fumble, answered
blocks.prompt: Write the two questions you would fumble today, and answer each in two sentences.

takeaways: Career changers get screened out for three reasons: retention doubt, jargon that cannot be mapped, and no proof of investment.
Every good answer has the same shape: where you are going, how you prepared, one accomplishment with a number.
Burnout is a true reason and a bad answer. It confirms the doubt they already have.
Weak answers name a quality. Strong answers describe an event with a number in it.
Knockout questions on the application form are the real automatic filter, so answer them honestly and in your own words.

tldr: Your bridge statement answers "why are you leaving clinical work?" in about forty-five seconds. It has three parts: pull, preparation, proof. Build it once, say it until it sounds like you, and use it everywhere.

blocks.text: You will answer "why are you leaving?" in every interview, on every screening call, and probably at a wedding. The question sounds like it wants the story of what went wrong. It wants to know whether you have thought this through and whether you are heading somewhere specific.
Build your answer from three parts and keep it under a minute

items: **Pull.** One sentence about where you are going. This is the sentence you wrote in lesson 1.8, and it is the only part that must be true to you rather than optimised.
**Preparation.** One sentence about what you have done to get ready. The artifact, the conversations, the course, the certificate if you took one.
**Proof.** One accomplishment from clinical work, with a real number, mapped onto a problem this role has in its first ninety days.

blocks.text: Said at a normal pace, the three parts take about forty-five seconds. Go longer and you start explaining, which sounds like justifying.
Turn what you are escaping into what you are moving toward
Push is what you are escaping and pull is what you are moving toward. The same fact can be either, depending on the sentence you put around it.

blocks.title: The same career, two framings
blocks.before: I'm burned out. The caseload was 62 kids across three buildings and I was doing notes at 9pm every night. I need out of the schools.
blocks.after: I want to work on the systems that decide how those 62 kids get served, rather than absorbing the consequences of them one session at a time. That's why I'm looking at program management.

blocks.title: Preparation, said badly and well
blocks.before: I've been researching the field and I'm a fast learner.
blocks.after: I rebuilt one of my own trainings as a Rise module, and I talked to three people doing this job about what their first month looked like.

blocks.title: Check your statement for five words
blocks.text: If any version of your statement contains burnout, paperwork, productivity, caseload size or administration, rewrite that sentence. Those words are all true. They also hand the interviewer the retention doubt for free.
Start from one of three openings that keep the doubt out
Three openings answer the question without handing over the doubt. Pick the one closest to your reason and fill in the brackets.

items.title: The pull
items.text: "I want to work on the systems that decide how patients get served, rather than absorbing the consequences one session at a time. This role is exactly that."

items.title: The scale
items.text: "I've helped [N] families one at a time for [N] years. I want the next [N] to reach more people than fit on a caseload, and [role] does that."

items.title: The part you'd keep
items.text: "What I'd keep from clinical work is [teaching clinicians / reading the chart], and in this role that's the whole job instead of a corner of it."

blocks.text: Say it out loud five times before a hiring manager hears it

Read it to a person or to a recorder five times. The first two will sound rehearsed. Around the fourth it sounds like something you think, which is what you need when the question arrives in a form you did not expect.

items.q: A screener asks, "So why leave speech therapy?" Which answer is a bridge statement?
options: The documentation and the productivity targets made the job unsustainable for me.
I want to train clinicians at scale. I rebuilt one of my trainings as a Rise module, and I trained 14 staff through an EMR switch.
I've researched the field carefully, and I'm a fast learner who is ready for a new challenge.
items.why: It has pull, preparation and a proof with a number in it. The first is push, and the third offers no evidence.

action.label: Save my statement
action.prompt: Fill in the three parts above, then say the whole thing out loud five times: to a partner, a friend, or your phone's voice recorder. When it stops sounding rehearsed, it is ready.
action.done: Saved. You will use that statement in every screening call from here.

takeaways: The bridge statement has three parts: where you are going, how you prepared, one accomplishment with a number.
Push is what you are escaping and pull is where you are going, and the same fact can usually be framed either way.
Forty-five seconds is about right. Longer and you start justifying.
Say it aloud five times before you say it to a hiring manager.

tldr: Practise five interview questions with a coach that knows your path and your own pull sentence. It tells you what landed, what read as escaping rather than moving toward, and where a number was missing.

blocks.text: Reading about interview answers and giving one are different skills, and the gap closes with repetition. Repetition is hard to arrange when the only people who would practise with you are the people you have not told yet.

So practise here first. The coach runs five questions for your path, in the order a real screen takes them, and gives you feedback after each answer. It knows your pull sentence from lesson 1.8 and the documented range for your path.
Answer out loud first, then type what you said

items: Answer out loud first, as if the question came from a person, then type roughly what you said. Typing a polished version you would never say aloud defeats the exercise.
Let it be bad the first time. The first run is diagnostic, not a performance.
Watch specifically for push language creeping in, and for answers with no number in them.
Run it again two days later. The second run is where it starts to feel like yours.

blocks.text: Listen for three habits that undersell you
Three habits mark a practice answer that needs another pass.

items.title: The word "just"
items.text: As in "I just did therapy."

items.title: Your title before your work
items.text: You explained your job title before you described what you did.

items.title: No result
items.text: You finished a story without saying what changed because of it.

blocks.text: we're all master's-level smart; I promise a lot of folks can do what I do.
The interview is the last place to undersell six years of training.
After a real interview, log the questions they asked you

The coach knows the questions most career changers get. It does not know what a hiring manager at a teletherapy platform asked last month. You will, and the next SLP interviewing there deserves to know.

items.q: You run the mock interview and your first answers come out rambling. What do you do next?
options: Type a polished version of each answer, so the feedback is on your best work.
Read the feedback, leave the answers as they are, and run it again in two days.
Stop, and come back once you have memorised stronger answers.
items.why: The first run is diagnostic, and the second run two days later is where the answers start to sound like yours.

items.q: In a practice answer you hear yourself say, "I just did therapy with kids who stutter." What do you fix first?
options: The word "just", and then you add what changed for those kids.
The mention of stuttering, because it is too clinical for a business interview.
Nothing, because the sentence is honest.
items.why: "Just" undersells the work, and a story with no stated result is one of the three habits to listen for.

action.label: Log five answers
action.prompt: Run the mock interview above end to end. Answer all five questions out loud, then type what you said. Read the feedback, then run it a second time in a day or two.
action.done: Five answered. Run it again whenever an interview is coming up. It never gets worse.

takeaways: Answer out loud, then type what you said. Writing a polished version you would not speak defeats the exercise.
The first run is diagnostic. Let it be bad.
Three habits mark an answer that needs work: the word just, explaining your title before your work, and no stated outcome.
Run it twice, a couple of days apart, before a real interview.

tldr: About thirty percent of people negotiate, most who ask get something, and employers rarely withdraw an offer over one polite counter. Anchor on the documented range for your path, then run the offer through eight checks before you answer.

blocks.text: Many SLPs have never negotiated pay, because school pay scales are published and the steps are fixed. That habit follows people out of the field and costs them.
Most people never ask, and most who ask get something

items.label: of people negotiate their offer at all (Pew 2023; ZipRecruiter Q4 2025)
of those who ask get something (Pew; Fidelity; ZipRecruiter)
more per year for negotiators in the one field study of new hires
of employers in a 2013 Salary.com survey said they expect candidates to negotiate

blocks.text: Employers rarely withdraw an offer because a candidate asked. In a 2024 study, hiring managers reported withdrawing fewer than two of about twenty-seven offers after a candidate negotiated, and candidates consistently overestimated that risk.

blocks.title: How solid this is
blocks.text: The dollar figures come from two modest samples of new hires and graduates, the withdrawal figure is what hiring managers report about themselves, and none of the surveys sampled SLPs. They show that asking is normal and usually pays. They do not promise a specific number.

blocks.title: How to ask so nobody takes offence

left.label: Raises the risk
items: Pushing on pay before they have made an offer
An ultimatum, or a competing offer you do not have
Reopening the number after you have said yes

right.label: Keeps it safe
items: Thank them, then ask once, with one number and a reason
Name a second option in case the base is fixed
Get the final terms in writing before you accept

blocks.text: Anchor on the range for the role, never on your clinical salary

Your current salary is the wrong reference point in both directions. If it is low for the new field you will underask, and if it is high you will sound unrealistic without the documented range behind you.

blocks.note: Your path's documented band. The middle of it is a reasonable anchor for a first non-clinical role with strong translated experience.

blocks.text: A growing list of states, California, Colorado, New York, Illinois and Washington among them, require the pay range on the job ad, and many states bar an employer from asking what you earn now. Both lists change several times a year, so look up a current pay-transparency tracker for your state. If the range is posted, negotiate inside it. If someone asks what you earn now, answer with the range you are looking for.
When you name a range, make the bottom a number you would accept.

blocks.title: When they ask what you're expecting
blocks.text: Based on what I've seen for this role, I've been looking at the [$X to $Y] range. I care about the whole package though, so if the base sits at the lower end I'd want to talk about [remote days / PTO / start date]. What range did you have budgeted?

blocks.title: Countering an offer
blocks.text: Thank you, I'm glad we got here. If we can get the base to [$Y], I'm ready to accept. That's inside the range [you posted / I've seen for this role], and it reflects [the specific thing: the clinical background the role asks for, the systems experience, the licence]. If the base is fixed, could we look at [a sign-on bonus / an early review / extra PTO]?

blocks.title: Asking for time
blocks.text: This is great news, thank you. Could I have until [day] to go through the full offer properly? I want to read the benefits and the details before I answer.
On a school contract, decide your start date before the interview

"When can you start?" is a question you answer before the interview. Read your contract for the resignation deadline and any fee for leaving mid-year, then say a real date. Hesitation in the room reads as doubt about the role.

blocks.title: Leaving a school contract mid-year can cost more than a fee
blocks.text: Some district contracts charge liquidated damages for leaving early, and some state education boards have suspended an educator certificate, school SLPs' among them, for resigning mid-contract without the district's release. Ask the district for a written release before you promise an earlier date.

blocks.title: "When can you start?", under a contract
blocks.text: My contract runs to [date], and I intend to honour it. I can start [the Monday after]. If the role needs someone sooner, I'd want to understand the timeline before I decide anything, because I'd rather tell you a real date than a hopeful one.
Ask about every part of the package, because base is only one of them

Base is rarely the whole number. In customer success the split runs roughly eighty-three percent base to seventeen percent variable in the one survey with published numbers, and in sales it moves toward half and half. Ask how much of a $110,000 offer is base before you set it against a fixed mortgage.

items.title: Variable pay
items.text: Ask what the target is, how it is measured, and when it pays. A target nobody hit last year is not income.

items.title: Equity, at startups
items.text: Grants typically vest over four years with a one-year cliff, so leaving inside twelve months leaves you nothing. Ask how many shares, out of how many total.

items.title: Sign-on bonus
items.text: A common tool when base is capped, though only about fifteen percent of new hires got one in late 2025. Ask whether you repay it if you leave early.

items.title: PTO, remote days, start date
items.text: All routinely negotiated, and often easier to move than base.

blocks.text: Find out what you forfeit by leaving before you resign
Nobody on the hiring side will raise what you leave behind, so read your own plan documents before you resign. A district pension two years from vesting is a number that belongs in the decision.

items: Ask your current HR in writing when the retirement match or pension vests, and what you forfeit by leaving on your date.
Ask the new employer for its share of the health premium and the date coverage starts.
Ask whether CEUs and licence renewal are reimbursed, and what the parental leave is.
Work out how a school-year salary maps onto twelve months before you compare the two numbers.

Check whether the role is salaried or hourly, and employee or contractor. Hourly employees are generally owed overtime past forty hours a week, and contractors get no benefits and pay their own payroll taxes.

blocks.text: Take a low offer only as a bridge with a date on it

Sometimes the offer sits below the range and they will not move. Decide on three things: the runway you calculated in lesson 5.5, whether the role has a ladder, and whether the title gets you the next job. Ask what people in this seat moved to, and when.

The clearest documented case is the research coordinator path at $48,000 to $72,000, which sits below where most SLPs already are. One person moved from a university coordinator role into pharma patient safety for ten thousand more, then another fifteen thousand eighteen months later. Taken as a destination, that job is a mistake. Taken as a bridge with a date on it, the same job is a strategy.
Run the offer through eight checks before you answer
An offer arrives with a deadline and a warm feeling that makes it hard to think. The checklist hands the decision to the version of you who set a floor and a runway before the phone rang.

Empty boxes are your questions for the follow-up call. Say the counter out loud once, to a person, before you say it to them. The sentence that feels outrageous in your head usually sounds reasonable in the air.
You have three answers: accept, counter, or decline

items.title: Accept
items.text: The number clears your runway, and the checks are ticked.

items.title: Counter, then accept
items.text: The role is right and a term or two is short. Ask for what is missing in one message.

items.title: Decline and keep going
items.text: The number sits below your runway, the role has no ladder, or you did not believe the manager. Declining costs a few weeks to save a year.

blocks.text: Get the offer in writing before you resign

items: Get it in writing before you resign anything. Base, title, start date, remote arrangement, variable pay terms.
Wait for any background or reference check the offer depends on to clear before you give notice.
Check the health coverage start date against your last day, and bridge the gap deliberately if there is one.
Give notice the way you would want it given to you, and do not use the resignation to explain the profession to anyone.
Tell the people who helped you. The person who answered your message in lesson 3.3 will want to know it worked.

blocks.text: Answer a no within a day, and keep the door open
When the no comes from a company you liked, reply within a day. A no on one role can be a maybe on the next, and the people who interviewed you are the warmest contacts you have at that company.

blocks.title: Answering a no from a company you liked
blocks.text:
Thank you for letting me know, and for the time your team gave me. I enjoyed the conversations about [specific thing], and I'd still like to work with you. If a similar role opens in the next few months, I'd welcome the chance to be considered, and I'll keep an eye on the careers page.

[Your name]

blocks.title: If you are the one who says no
blocks.text: A declined offer means the process works. You got to an offer, so the résumé, the statement and the artifact are all doing their jobs. Log it in the tracker and keep the pace.

items.q: A recruiter calls with an offer at the bottom of the posted range and asks for an answer today. What do you do?
options: Accept on the call, so the offer cannot be withdrawn.
Thank them, ask for the details in writing and until a named day, then counter once inside the range.
Say another company has offered more, to see whether they move.
items.why: Asking for time and countering once with a reason is expected, and employers rarely withdraw an offer for it. A bluff is the kind of ask that raises the risk.

items.q: The base is below your path's range, and the hiring manager says it is fixed. What is your next move?
options: Decline at once, because a low base means a bad employer.
Ask about a sign-on bonus, an early review or extra PTO, then weigh the offer against your runway and the role's ladder.
Accept, and plan to reopen the salary in your first month.
items.why: A fixed base leaves other terms to ask for, and your runway and the ladder decide whether a low first number works as a bridge.

blocks.text: When you do accept, come back and mark it here.

action.label: I have an offer
action.prompt: Run the offer through the eight checks above. Ask for anything that is missing, in one message. Then, whichever way you decide, mark it here.
action.done: Marked. Whatever you decided, you got to a real offer from a standing start. Tell somebody.

takeaways: About thirty percent of people negotiate, and two thirds or more of those who ask get something.
Ask once, after the offer, with one number and a reason. Anchor on the documented range for the path, never on your clinical salary.
A below-range first offer can still be right if the role has a ladder and you put a date on it.
On a school contract, read the resignation terms and get a written release before you promise an early start date.
Get everything in writing before resigning, and check the coverage start date against your last day.

tldr: One documented transition took 113 tailored applications, 7 interviews and 1 offer over eleven months. Track the numbers and silence becomes a rate you can work with.

blocks.text: Around week six the silence starts to feel personal, so look at the numbers from people who got where you are going.
Another SLP sent more than five hundred applications over six months before landing a fully remote analyst role above their clinical salary, and a third describes fourteen months of daily effort.
I applied to more than 500 jobs. I built a portfolio, earned certifications, rewrote my resume and cover letters dozens of times
Apply in the first two days, because every posting draws a crowd

Postings average around 242 applications each, roughly double what they drew in 2022, and the applications that get read are mostly the ones from a posting's first day or two. A thoughtful application sent on day one beats a perfect one sent on day nine.
Track four numbers, and let the ratio show which stage is broken

blocks.title: The whole dashboard

blocks.text: Applications sent, screens, interviews and offers are the entire dashboard. Once you have a few dozen applications logged, the ratio between two neighbouring numbers tells you which stage is broken.

items.title: Applications, no screens
items.text: The résumé still reads clinical, the roles sit a level too senior, or you are applying cold with no referral. Back to lessons 4.2 and 3.6.

items.title: Screens, no interviews
items.text: The bridge statement is doing the wrong work, usually push instead of pull. Lesson 6.2.

items.title: Interviews, no offers
items.text: Usually the proof problem. One thing you built (lesson 5.2) fixes more of this than another certificate will.

items.title: Nothing for four weeks
items.text: Volume. The documented search above averaged about ten tailored applications a month. Three a month is too few to give you a rate.

blocks.text: Keep the list on your people and applications page, the one you started in lesson 4.7, because the four numbers only mean something next to each other.
Two questions on the form stop people, and both have a standard answer

items.title: "Contact your current employer?"
items.text: "No" is a complete answer, and the normal one for anyone still employed. Offer a past supervisor, a mentor, or a colleague who already left.

items.title: "Expected salary"
items.text: In a text box, write "negotiable". In a number box, enter one inside the posted range, or the middle of your path's documented band. Never your clinical salary.

blocks.text: Employers usually check references late, around the final interview or the offer. Line up two or three people now, and hand over their names when you are asked.
Send a thank-you the same day, then follow up on their timeline

blocks.title: After the interview

items.label: Same day
items.note: thank them, name one thing you took away, say you want the role

items.label: Their date passes
items.note: check in the next day: day fifteen if they said two weeks

blocks.text: Wait for the timeline they gave you. If they said two weeks, write on day fifteen, not day five. More than three messages reads as pressure, and the offer you are waiting on should not be the only one you are working.

blocks.title: The follow-up, when the timeline has passed
blocks.text: Hi [Name], you mentioned you'd have an update by [date], so I wanted to check in. I'm still very interested in the [title] role and happy to send anything else that would help. Is there a revised timeline I should work to?
Count rejections as a rate, and expect a slower pace if you are burnt out

blocks.title: Rejection at this stage is a volume statistic
blocks.text: Seven interviews out of 113 applications is a six percent rate, and that person is now employed. The maths only works if you keep feeding it, which is easier when you can see the numbers instead of feeling them.

Job searching while burnt out is harder, because planning and follow-through are the executive functions a burnt-out brain struggles to use. If your pace is slower than the numbers above, that tells you about your capacity this month. It says nothing about your prospects.

items.q: You have sent 40 tailored applications in two months and had no screening calls. What do you change first?
options: Your interview answers, with another run of the mock interview.
The résumé's language, and you ask a contact for a referral before the next application.
Nothing, because rejection is a volume statistic.
items.why: Applications with no screens point at a résumé that reads clinical or at applying cold, the stage before any interview answer matters.

items.q: A form has a required number box for expected salary, and the posting lists a range. What goes in the box?
options: Your current clinical salary, so that you look honest.
A number inside the posted range.

items.why: A number inside the posted range keeps you in the running, and your clinical salary anchors you to the wrong field.

takeaways: One documented transition: 113 applications, 7 interviews, 1 offer, eleven months.
Postings average around 242 applicants, so a day-one application beats a perfect day-nine one.
Track applications, screens, interviews and offers, because the ratio between them tells you which stage is broken.
On a form, say no to contacting your current employer, and put a number from the posted range in the salary box.
Rejection at this stage is a volume statistic, and the maths only works if you keep feeding it.
